title: Bodyweight Training
subtitle: Use leverage, support, range, and tempo to build strength almost anywhere

blocks.text: This lesson is general education, not diagnosis, treatment or rehab. Fill out CSEP’s Get Active Questionnaire before a big increase in activity and follow what it says. Get qualified advice for a recent injury or surgery, repeated falls, a joint that gives way, pain, weakness or numbness you can’t explain, pregnancy or postpartum concerns, or a health condition that changes how you exercise. Stop and get urgent medical help for chest pressure or pain, fainting, severe or unusual shortness of breath, sudden nerve symptoms, a serious fall, or suddenly being unable to put weight on a leg.
Your body provides the resistance, but it doesn’t come with a tiny instruction manual taped to the elbow. This lesson gives you five controls for choosing the right level.
Build real strength with nothing but your body and a sturdy chair.
blocks.detail: Knowing how to make any move easier or harder means you can train anywhere, at exactly the right level.
blocks.extra: Section 03 shows you the five controls that set the difficulty.

blocks.text: Bodyweight training uses your own mass and gravity to challenge your muscles. Chair rises, wall push-ups, step-ups, bridges, calf raises and getting down to the floor and up again are familiar examples. The same move can feel gentle or hard depending on your position and leverage.

The goal isn’t to prove you can exercise without equipment. Choose enough resistance for useful, controlled work. A countertop push-up may do far more for you than a floor push-up that changes shape halfway down.
Give your training a destination: getting up from a low chair, climbing stairs, pushing a heavy door or getting down to the floor and back up with control.
Change the setup before you give up on an exercise. Height, support, stance and range can turn one move into several useful levels.

items.title: “Bodyweight training is always easy.”
items.text: A move can be gentle or extremely hard. Leverage, range, speed, support and working one limb at a time all change the challenge.

blocks.text: Name your training target
Finish this sentence: “I want bodyweight training to help me __________.”
Support. A wall push-up gives more support than a floor push-up. A chair or railing can help with a squat, step, balance task or getting down to the floor.
Body angle and range. Your angle changes how much of your weight the muscles handle. Range changes how far your joints move.
Tempo and reps. Tempo, or how slowly you move, changes how long the muscles work. Reps change the total amount of work.

Adjust one control at a time. If a chair rise is too hard, use a higher seat or your hands. When it gets easy, lower more slowly or use a slightly lower, sturdy seat. Fitness progress is often a small furniture adjustment wearing sensible shoes.
Write down which control you changed, so you know why the exercise got harder or easier.

items.title: “A repetition only counts if it reaches a standard depth.”
items.text: Useful range depends on the person, the task, control, how your joints feel and any professional advice.

sections.title: Learn the Pattern, Then Cover the Movement Jobs

blocks.text: Start with a steady version that lets you breathe normally and repeat good form. Use a chair rise for a squat, a wall or countertop for a push, a supported hinge or bridge for the hips, and a bird dog, raised plank or dead bug for core control.
A balanced routine can include a squat-type move, a hinge-type move, a push, a pull, a step or one-leg move, and core control. You don’t need every pattern in every session.

Pulling is the hardest to do without equipment. Use a station built for it, supervised equipment where it’s allowed or a gym machine. A resistance band with a proper anchor also works. Don’t pull on tables, doors, railings or fixtures that aren’t built for exercise. This lesson should solve problems, not recruit the dining table into a risky internship.
Bodyweight-only plans often skip pulling. Use proper equipment or qualified advice, not a questionable household anchor.

sections.title: Use Effort, Recovery, and One-Step Progression

blocks.text: Choose a version that feels hard near the end of a set while your form stays controlled. Rest enough to do it well again. Stop when your speed, alignment, balance or breathing changes noticeably, leaving a few good reps in reserve while you learn.

Progress by adding a controlled rep, more range, less support, a harder body angle, a slower lowering, a pause or another set. Change one thing, then check how you feel later that day and the next morning.
More soreness doesn’t mean a better workout. Progress shows up as better control, work you can repeat, a harder version that suits you or an easier daily task.

items.title: “Muscle soreness is required for progress.”
items.text: Soreness varies with how new the work is, how much you did, recovery and the person. Good training doesn’t need to make the stairs file a complaint.

sections.title: Marcus Finds His Correct Starting Level

blocks.text: Kwame finds his real starting level
paragraphs: Kwame, 36, drove a delivery truck in Regina and saved a thirty-day push-up challenge on his phone. Day one asked for more floor push-ups than he could control. He forced out a few with his hips sagging, felt sore and embarrassed, and avoided the plan for a week. The calendar stayed extremely motivated on his behalf.
When the app sent him a “Don’t give up!” reminder, he had a choice. He could try day one again and hope his body had changed, or he could find a starting level he could do well. He chose the second.
He started over with countertop push-ups, chair rises, supported split squats, bridges and a raised plank against the counter. Twice a week, he wrote down the surface height, his range and his reps.

Once every rep came with steady breathing, he moved the push-up to a slightly lower surface: from the counter to the back of a sturdy couch. For chair rises, he slowed the lowering before trying a lower seat. Only one control changed at a time.
In week five, a coworker challenged him to a floor push-up contest on their lunch break. Kwame was tempted. He did three clean ones, stopped while his form was still good and laughed off the loss.

After eight weeks, he did his push-ups from a low step and carried groceries up to his third-floor apartment with fewer stops. He never finished the internet challenge. He built a routine he could keep going.

blocks.text: “Push-up” is an incomplete note. Write down the surface height, range, tempo and reps.
Start at the right level, and progress takes care of itself.
blocks.detail: Choosing a version you can do well, then changing one thing at a time, builds strength without the setbacks.
blocks.extra: Section 07 helps you build a short session you can repeat.

blocks.text: Start with a few minutes of easy movement and practise the ranges you’ll use. Choose four or five patterns. Do one or more controlled sets, rest as needed and finish before your technique gets unreliable.

A simple session might include chair rises, countertop push-ups, supported split squats, bridges and core control. Add safe pulling when you have suitable equipment. Keep the same routine long enough to learn it.

Bodyweight training builds strength, but it doesn’t replace cardio, balance practice, mobility, sleep or recovery. The lessons in this course work best as one toolkit, not separate plans competing for the same Tuesday evening.

sections.title: Read Symptoms and Adapt the Environment

blocks.text: Clear the floor, steady your chairs, keep pets and cords out of the way, wear suitable shoes and keep support within reach. Avoid wobbly furniture, slippery floors and makeshift hanging or pulling setups.

Stop for sharp or worsening pain, numbness, weakness that keeps getting worse, dizziness, unusual shortness of breath, a joint that gives way, losing your balance or symptoms that change how you normally move. Get a qualified check if symptoms last or affect your daily life.
This section has no humour, because falls, nerve symptoms, serious pain and equipment failure need clear decisions.

items.title: “Bodyweight exercise is automatically safer than external weights.”
items.text: Falls, the wrong leverage, poor support, too much work and unstable surfaces can still cause injury.

blocks.text: A useful set ends before your position, balance, breathing or range gets unreliable.

Help may be available from CSEP professionals, physiotherapists, kinesiologists, rec centres, community health programs, Indigenous health organizations, campuses, seniors’ programs and adapted exercise services. Coverage, referrals, regulation, eligibility, facility rules and wait times vary by province and territory.

A qualified professional can help you pick safe support, range and next steps. Physiotherapists can assess pain and movement problems. Occupational therapists can help you adapt daily tasks and your home.
Key takeaway
Bodyweight training is resistance you can adjust. Use support, angle, range, tempo and reps to pick a controlled level, cover the useful movement patterns and progress one thing at a time.
Take a photo of your setup, with no people or private details in it. Future you can then see which countertop you used and where your feet went.

items.title: What makes bodyweight exercise adjustable?
items.detail: Leverage, position, support, range, tempo, repetitions, and gravity change the resistance.

items.title: Name the five difficulty controls.
items.detail: Support, body angle, range, tempo, and repetitions.

items.title: Why begin with a stable variation?
items.detail: It allows repeatable form, steady breathing, balance, and a suitable starting dose.

items.title: Why can pulling be difficult in a bodyweight-only plan?
items.detail: Safe pulling usually needs suitable equipment or an approved structure; household furniture may be unstable.

items.title: Give four ways to progress.
items.detail: Add a repetition, increase range, reduce support, change angle, slow the lowering, add a pause, or add a set.

items.title: What changed Marcus's results?
items.detail: He chose controlled variations, recorded his setup, and progressed one feature at a time.

items.title: Why is soreness not the main score?
items.detail: Soreness reflects novelty and dose, not necessarily useful progress. Control and function are better measures.

items.title: Name two environmental safety checks.
items.detail: Clear cords, stabilize chairs, use a non-slip surface, manage pets, wear suitable footwear, or keep support nearby.

blocks.text: Complete the relevant safety screen. Choose four movements and record each exact variation. Complete one controlled session, note the response, and schedule the next session before adding difficulty.
Skip medical details and symptoms in this form. Just record the plan.

items.title: Body angle
items.text: The position of the body relative to gravity or a support surface.

items.title: Bodyweight training
items.text: Resistance exercise that mainly uses the person's mass and gravity.

items.title: Leverage
items.text: How body position and limb length change the difficulty of a movement.

items.title: Repetitions in reserve
items.text: An estimate of how many controlled repetitions remain before technique fails.

items.title: Tempo
items.text: The speed and timing of each part of a repetition.
